latest.title: Badenoch quizzes Burnham at PMQs over tuition fee bill in deal with EU – UK politics live
latest.summary: The prime minister says the government is bringing forward legislation for the three deals announced last week Diane Taylor is a Guardian reporter who covers migration. Britons get many of the facts about migration wrong and Reform UK voters are the group who get these facts most wrong, according to new research published today by King’s College University and YouGov. Among Reform UK supporters, 57% think net migration rose significantly in the year to June 2025, compared with 11% of Labour supporters and 8% of Greens. Eight in 10 Reform supporters think that asylum seekers are prioritised for social housing, compared with 21% of Green supporters. It is wrong to believe that if we could only correct misperceptions, we would automatically reduce concerns about immigration or policy preferences – because that misdiagnoses a large part of the cause, that these divides are partly driven by deep differences in values and identity. Continue reading...

Business.title: Campaigners call for emergency government support as average annual energy bill in Britain set to hit £2,166 – business live
Business.summary: Regulator Ofgem announces that the typical annual gas and electricity bill will rise by 26% in January – described as ‘deeply worrying’ by campaigners Hannah Webster , senior economist at the think tank New Economics Foundation , also called for other measures. The price cap increase will be difficult news for households to bear, especially during the winter when our energy needs and bills are higher. The government’s current support measures don’t match the reality of rising costs and squeezed household finances. The £100 payment announced at the budget won’t cover the increase that’s coming, nor is it available to every household. According to NEF analysis, one million low-income households will miss out. Today’s price cap rise shows how exposed households remain to imported energy - the answer is to generate more at home. Biomethane, made from farms and food waste, is already flowing through our grid - enough to heat around a million homes - but NESO [National Energy System Operator] has just cut its outlook for biomethane because of policy uncertainty. Those receiving a placebo experienced no significant improvement. The discovery points to a promising, low-cost natural approach to managing mildly elevated blood pressure.

Science.title: Physicists trap antimatter in a breakthrough that could explain why the universe exists

Culture.title: Mow down an alligator to the music of Mahler! I love how Grand Theft Auto VI went crazy for classical
Culture.summary: Rob a bank to the sound of Sibelius, steal a chopper listening to Liszt … piano sensation Yuja Wang is one of the surprise treats of GTA VI – and her thrilling musical choices made me crash into a G-Wagen I blame Yuja Wang for crashing my car. You know how it is, you’re cruising as fast you can on the freeway, listening to Symphony FM. And then DJ Yuja says: “It’s afternoon here in Vice City: for the worst of you, the day is just starting. Maybe the next piece will inspire you to turn your life around.” And then she played Tchaikovsky – the finale of the Fifth Symphony – and I just lost it to the music. The energy and tempest of the finale turned me into a driving maniac, and I ended up crashing into a G-Wagen down a one-way street as the minor-key maelstrom took over. Thanks Yuja. I’ll send you the repair bill. Such are the hazards of discovering that among the 24 stations you can listen to in Grand Theft Auto VI – and not only in your car – is Symphony FM, hosted by the in-game Yuja, who really is the real-life piano superstar Yuja Wang . And in choosing her “favourite pieces and curating a playlist for players to discover”, she’s put together a set of 16 pieces that only she could have come up with. Continue reading...

Culture.title: ‘I said no thanks to the casting couch. But other actresses had problems’: Jane Alexander on 50 years of stardom
Culture.summary: The Great White Hope, All the President’s Men, Kramer vs Kramer … Alexander has a CV most actors can only dream of. She talks us through the highs and lows – including a ‘beautiful’ encounter with Muhammad Ali Jane Alexander will never forget the play that won her a Tony award, a husband and her first film role. The Great White Hope, which ran on Broadway from 1968 to 1970, was based on the life of Black boxer Jack Johnson, who in 1908 became world heavyweight champion in segregated America. Alexander played Eleanor, a white woman married to an African American boxer also called Jack, at a time when interracial marriages were still illegal in many states. Decades later, when the play opened, the US supreme court had only recently struck down all remaining bans – and Alexander received hate mail and death threats for the role. Continue reading...

Culture.title: ‘I had to reject a lot of shame’: Michaela Yearwood-Dan on queerness, Catholicism and her extravagant artist dinner parties
Culture.summary: The artist adorns her luscious paintings with diaristic notes and confessions. Ahead of an exuberant new show she discusses their unique creation method – and the hunt for her missing cat The artist Michaela Yearwood-Dan is on the hunt for her missing cat. Pinto disappeared from her home in east London a couple of weeks ago and has so far defied the forecasts of tarot readings and the “witchy ladies” predicting his return. A lost pet is not the only thing she’s searching for. “I’m at a stage of life where I’m looking for answers” she says on the eve of her exhibition The Practice of Liberation, at Towner Eastbourne. Her other, more existential questions are those of many women in their early 30s: “Do I want to have children? How do I want to have children? What does my future look like?” She is “big into astrology”, but recently her thoughts have turned to her Catholic upbringing in south London, which serves as a large theme of her exhibition, which debuted at the Whitworth Gallery in Manchester earlier this year. Religious ritual has always appealed to her, and her show uses paintings, ceramics and a musical composition by her friend and longstanding collaborator Alex Gruz to evoke the ritual space of a church. Continue reading...

Culture.title: Post your questions for Carl Cox
Culture.summary: Ahead of him rounding out the year at a huge London show, the DJ legend will join us to answer your questions Beatifically smiling as he sends another packed dancefloor into raptures, Carl Cox is one of the most enduring and reliably euphoria-inducing figures in UK club culture history. As he prepares to close out the current season at Drumsheds, the UK’s biggest nightclub, and looks towards a return of his residency at Ibiza nightclub Unvrs, he will join us to answer your questions. Known for playing a banging yet nuanced blend of house and techno, Cox’s career stretches back to the age of 10, learning his craft growing up in London and later Brighton, funding nights out by trimming his neighbours’ hedges. As Chicago house, Detroit techno and other new styles hit the UK, Cox was primed to receive them: fluidly mixing across three decks at once, he immersed himself in both the illegal rave scene and the new wave of nightclubs cropping up to showcase this music.
